summary: Describes the guidelines and procedures for forming and running IETF working groups. It covers how groups are chartered, how chairs work, how consensus is reached and how groups close. It is a Best Current Practice and has since been updated by several later documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2418 is the handbook for IETF working groups. It explains how a group gets a charter, how it makes decisions by rough consensus, who fills the roles of chair and editor, and how its documents move forward toward becoming RFCs.

subtitle: The rulebook for how IETF working groups are formed, run, staffed and closed down.

tldr.problem: The IETF does its standards work in working groups, and those groups need shared rules for how they start, how they decide things, who does what, and when they stop.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2418 sets out a chartering process reviewed by the IAB and approved by the IESG, decision-making by rough consensus, open mailing lists and sessions, defined staff roles such as the Chair, and a path from Internet-Draft to RFC.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 25) that obsoletes RFC 1603. Later RFCs, namely 3934, 7475, 7776, 8717, 9141 and 9945, update it, so read it together with them.

facts.value: At least two weeks before a session

sections.title: Working Groups in the IETF
sections.content:
The IETF develops Internet Standards in working groups (WGs). Working groups are grouped into areas, each managed by one or two Area Directors (ADs), who together with the IETF Chair form the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). There is no formal IETF membership: participation is open to all and happens by on-line contribution, face-to-face sessions, or both.

This RFC describes how working groups are formed and operated, and the relationship between working group participants and the IESG. It uses RFC 2119 key words (MUST, SHOULD and so on) to make the process clear. It obsoletes RFC 1603.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is an open community that writes Internet standards through teams called working groups. This document explains the ground rules for those teams.

sections.title: Forming a Working Group
sections.content:
Anyone who wants to create a working group must obtain the advice and consent of the relevant Area Director and follow the formal steps. The ADs and IESG judge whether the topic is clear and relevant, the goals achievable, whether the work overlaps another group, and whether enough people are willing to do the work.

A working group needs a charter, negotiated between a prospective Chair and the Area Director and finally approved by the IESG with advice from the IAB. A charter lists administrative information, the direction and objectives, and a set of milestones with time frames. The charter must give the group a name with an acronym of at most eight printable ASCII characters, one or more Chairs (generally limited to two), a responsible Area Director, and a general Internet mailing list with a public archive.

Before forming a group, an AD may hold an exploratory Birds of a Feather (BOF) session. A BOF on a topic is generally held once and is never permitted to meet three times.
sections.plainLanguage: To start a group, someone writes a charter with clear goals and deadlines. The Area Director and the IESG review it. If the idea is uncertain, an open exploratory meeting (a BOF) may be held first.

sections.title: Running a Working Group
sections.content:
Working groups are autonomous within the IETF's basic requirements for open and fair participation. The core rule is that agreement is reached by rough consensus. Rough consensus does not require everyone to agree; the dominant view prevails, and 51 percent does not qualify, while 99 percent is better than rough. The Chair decides whether rough consensus has been reached.

Much of the work happens on the mailing list. The Chair must publish a draft agenda well before each session, sessions must be reported in minutes, and decisions reached in a face-to-face meeting on topics not discussed on the list must be reviewed on the list. A two-week last-call period is normally enough to verify consensus.

Important decisions should be summarized and archived, and the Chair may set aside input that is old, minor, out of scope, or on a topic the group has not yet opened. Disputes are resolved through the IETF's open review and appeal process.
sections.plainLanguage: The group works mostly by email and periodic meetings. It aims for rough consensus, meaning broad agreement rather than a bare majority, and the Chair judges whether that point has been reached.

sections.title: Termination and Rechartering
sections.content:
Working groups are expected to be short-lived and are disbanded once their tasks are complete. If a group produces a Proposed or Draft Standard, it often becomes dormant rather than disbanding, keeping its mailing list available while the work advances.

If a group cannot finish its chartered work, the Area Director, after consulting the group, may recharter it, choose new Chairs, or disband it. Rechartering a group (other than revising milestones) follows the same process as the initial chartering, with approval by the IESG and IAB. If the group disagrees with the Area Director's choice, it may appeal to the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: Groups close when their work is done. If the work cannot be finished as planned, the Area Director can refocus the group, replace its Chairs, or shut it down.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
Working groups rely on people filling specific roles. The WG Chair makes forward progress through a fair and open process, plans and announces sessions, moderates the mailing list, distributes the workload, reports to the Area Director after each session, and documents the implementations that qualify a specification for advancement.

A Secretary records decisions and takes minutes. A Document Editor ensures the document reflects the group's decisions; by general practice the Chair and Editor are different people. A Facilitator may manage the process when meetings become divisive, and a design team may develop a proposal, subject to the whole group's approval.

Area Directors ensure their working groups produce coherent, coordinated and timely output, and must agree to the people filling the Chair and Consultant roles.
sections.plainLanguage: Chairs keep things moving and fair, secretaries write minutes, and editors write the documents. Area Directors oversee the groups in their area.

sections.title: Working Group Documents
sections.content:
Documents discussed at a session should be available as Internet-Drafts at least two weeks before the session starts. A document that misses that deadline can only be discussed with the Chair's specific approval.

Work normally proceeds from an Internet-Draft to a working group Last-Call, then to submission for publication as an RFC. The Chair and Document Editor work with the RFC Editor to ensure the document conforms to publication requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Drafts must be posted well before a meeting so people can read them, and they move forward only after the group has reviewed them.
